newsitem.title: BOSNIA: Moslems want voting on Serb territory invalidated.
newsitem.headline: Moslems want voting on Serb territory invalidated.

text.p: Bosnia's Moslem-led central government has urged the Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE) to invalidate the results of elections on Serb territory even before they are held.
The OSCE dismissed the demand and diplomats described it as a ploy by the Bosnian government to grab a post-election advantage over its wartime Serb enemies.

General elections are to be held across Bosnia on September 14 to reunify Moslem, Serb and Croat-dominated sectors carved out in war but campaign abuses by nationalist parties have ruled out a free and fair vote in much of the country.
Human-rights monitors say irregularities have been especially grave on separatist Serb republic territory.
Bosnia's U.N. Ambassador Muhamed Sacirbey said:
"The pending elections and their results within the Serb Republic cannot be considered democratic, neither free nor fair, nor legally valid," Sacirbey said.
"For these and other reasons, we request that the complete results of such elections in the Serb Republic be declared null and void and legally invalid," he said.
In Sarajevo, OSCE spokesman Thomas Leary responded: "It would be premature to rule on the validity of voting in the Serb Republic before they take place."
The elections are widely expected to yield an SDS majority in the half of Bosnia under Serb rule.
OSCE-Bosnia director Robert Frowick has conceded that the election conditions are deeply flawed but says the balloting must be held according to the schedule set by Dayton.
Carl Bildt, International High Representative in Bosnia, unveiled a plan on Saturday for the post-election period.

Pre-existing separate governing bodies would have only "administrative caretaker functions" to ensure new power-sharing institutions were set up as swiftly as possible, Bildt spokesman Colum Murphy said.
The new multi-ethnic presidency -- one Moslem, one Serb and one Croat -- would meet four days and the new House of Representatives 10 days after the elections are certified.

A "Quick-Start Package" with minimum legislation to run a joint state, including a 1997 budget and law on international economic relations, should be passed by the House at its first session in November, according to Bildt's plan.
